transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-29T15:00:00Z
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (CTO, Acuity Health), Tom Rivers (SRE Lead), Elena Morales (Platform Eng)

Summary:
Quick hands-on lab focused on tuning continuous-batching scheduler knobs: adaptive window sizing, max_num_seqs, token ceilings/throttles, KV cache prefetch/warmup, and quantization fallback behavior for Acuity's peaky telehealth inference workload. Goal: reduce 95/99 tail without blowing token cost.

Topics:
- workload profile and seq length distribution
- scheduler knob interplay (window_ms vs max_num_seqs vs priority slots)
- token ceiling and fair-share throttling
- KV cache prefetch / warmstart strategies for VPC/on-prem environments
- int8/quant fallback safety during bursts
- measurement plan and artifacts (bench CSV, latency histograms)

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: ok everyone thanks for joining, want to dive straight into the workload you sent — Maya can you remind us of the key SLA you care about and the burst patterns?
[00:18] Maya: yeah, sure. our primary is 95th latency under 250ms for short chat completions; we have large bursts at the top of each hour when appointment reminders hit, like 5k rps for 15s, then long tail at 50-100 rps.
[00:36] Tom: and to add, our sequences are bimodal — ~60% short (<=32 tokens) and ~30% medium (100-300 tokens) and a handful of long ones up to 2k. costs scale real fast when those long seqs go through.
[00:55] Priya: okay that distribution is exactly the friction point. continuous batching by itself helps average cost but the tail and long seqs can hold the scheduler. so we want adaptive windowing + max_num_seqs to limit head-of-line blocking.
[01:14] Elena: couple questions: we are on an on-prem-ish VPC peered setup, KV cache can't be persisted across cold restarts the same way you do in hosted, right? so warmup matters.
[01:31] Priya: correct, in private deployments you control KV warmstart. we usually recommend a prefetching heartbeat: small synthetic 'prime' requests that reconstruct kv entries for the active model shards prior to peak windows.
[01:47] Speaker 1: uh-huh, that makes sense, is that something you automate?
[01:52] Priya: kind of — Redwood has a prefetch runner that can be scheduled; for on-prem we ship a helper script. but careful: prefetch itself consumes tokens and can change the scheduler dynamics, so you set it to low-priority or to dedicated prewarming slots.
[02:12] Jordan: let's talk knobs. Priya, can you list the ones we tweak in order of impact?
[02:18] Priya: sure — window_ms (the batching window), max_num_seqs (per-batch sequence cap), token_ceiling (max tokens per request accepted), priority_slots (reserved high-priority lanes), and token_fairness (per-customer token rate limiter). window_ms trades off latency vs throughput; increase it to let more seqs aggregate but it increases p95. max_num_seqs prevents one batch from being dominated by long sequences. token_ceiling short-circuits heavy tail requests so they don't block others.
[02:46] Maya: can you give concrete starting values for our traces?
[02:49] Priya: with your mix I'd start window_ms=12ms, max_num_seqs=24, token_ceiling=512 for general paths; then carve 2 priority_slots for low-latency interactive traffic. those are starting heuristics — we will tune with your trace.
[03:07] Tom: why 12ms vs your default 8 or 25?
[03:11] Priya: 12ms often hits a sweet spot on GPUs we tested — enough time to form meaningful batches for short seqs without adding much latency. 8ms can be too small for peaks to amortize, 25ms reduces p50 but causes p95 drift. again, depends on arrival shape.
[03:29] Jordan: what about continuous batching and max_num_seqs interplay — if a very long sequence arrives and hoards tokens, will it be limited by max_num_seqs?
[03:38] Priya: yes, max_num_seqs limits how many sequences of any length a single batch may contain; but a long sequence can still push tokens — that's why we have token_ceiling plus active eviction or preemption in the scheduler. we also have a per-request token cap that we enforce early to avoid oversized requests entering the batch.
[03:57] Elena: we have a user-facing policy that sometimes requires completion beyond 512 tokens for transcripts. if we cap at 512 we'll truncate. any safer alternative?
[04:06] Priya: two options — allow long requests but route them to a dedicated pool with larger max_num_seqs and higher cost, or accept them but classify as low-priority and let them fall back to a queued path. both maintain interactive p95.
[04:22] Maya: what about quantization? we've considered int8 to save cost but worried about quality regression during bursts when fallback to fp16 might flip.
[04:32] Priya: common pattern: run quantized model by default; detect quality regressions via a small cohort of golden prompts before large rollout. operationally, on heavy bursts quantized path might saturate memory differently — that's where the runtime can fallback to float16 model variants if latency degrades. we can configure an automatic fallback threshold (e.g., if p95 > 400ms or coherence score drops).
[04:58] Tom: does fallback restart sessions or invalidate KV cache?
[05:02] Priya: no, we keep KV cache format compatible across quant variants where possible; but sometimes we need to rebuild on fallback — that's why we recommend ephemeral prewarming on fallback trigger to avoid long cold penalties.
[05:18] Jordan: let's sketch measurement plan: Priya will run the workload on dev cluster with three configs — baseline, adaptive-window, and dedicated-long-pool. collect p50/p95/p99, token cost, and KV hitrates. agreed?
[05:33] Maya: yes, and please include cold vs warm start curves. our main fear is a long sequence causing tail to spike after a cold restart.
[05:41] Priya: noted. we'll also instrument per-batch composition logs so you can see how many long seqs per batch and whether max_num_seqs bound is hit.
[05:53] Speaker 2: random thought — what if we pre-classify requests and send long ones straight to a different queue?
[05:58] Priya: that's actually effective: pre-routing by length + priority keeps short interactive responses fast. we often combine that with token-ceil checks and per-route quotas.
[06:09] Jordan: on the VPC side, Tom mentioned egress — any constraints that should change prefetch cadence?
[06:15] Tom: egress to Redwood control plane needs to go through our proxy and we have 100Mbps burst limits during certain windows. prefetch can be tuned to stagger workers so we don't exceed that.
[06:26] Priya: good catch — we'll make prefetch heartbeat adaptive based on observed bandwidth consumption. also suggest prefetch from inside the VPC to minimize external calls — the on-prem helper supports local priming.
[06:37] Elena: what's the recommended KV warmup volume? do you prime all embeddings or only active keys?
[06:43] Priya: prime active keys only and use an LRU eviction policy. for your topology, priming the top 20% most accessed keys covers ~85% hits in our tests. exact numbers will come from your trace.
[06:58] Jordan: small callout — during bench we'll want to toggle token_fairness to see the effect on multi-tenant fairness and cost.
[07:06] Priya: yes, we will. also capture scheduler metrics: batch sizes, wait times, eviction counts, and preemption events.
[07:15] Maya: how long do you expect the initial bench to take?
[07:18] Priya: if you give traces, we can do a 1-hour run to get stable p99 and cost numbers — that should be enough to decide initial knobs.
[07:26] Jordan: ok next steps recap — Redwood runs bench, Acuity provides trace, SE provides config diffs and prefetch script, schedule follow up. any other concerns?
[07:36] Tom: just one — regression testing for quality if you switch quantization midstream, please include an eval set.
[07:42] Priya: will do, we'll run the golden prompt checks before and after quant changes.
[07:47] Maya: great thanks.
[07:50] Jordan: thanks all, we'll email artifacts and calendar invite for the 2h lab.

End of transcript.
